title: I Lived in the Rainiest Village on Earth. My Socks Didn't.
question: Why do people live in Mawsynram?
message: This video tells curious adults that people live in one of the rainiest places on Earth because it is the Khasi people's home, and they have built a whole way of life, from walking roofs to bridges that grow, around the rain.
angle: People live in Mawsynram because it is the long-standing home of Khasi families who have shaped their houses, clothes, crops and even their bridges around the monsoon, despite rain measured in metres, landslides on the only road, power cuts, and, strangely, dry-season water shortages.

scenes.narration: The place is Mawsynram, a cluster of hamlets in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in northeast India. The World Meteorological Organization lists it as the record for the greatest average yearly rainfall in Asia. Other places, including nearby Cherrapunji and a couple of towns in Colombia, have their own claims, so the title is disputed. Either way, it rains here like the sky has a deadline. And yet Khasi families have lived in these hills for generations, and many say they would not live anywhere else. By the end of this trip I understood why. I also understood that I should have packed more socks. A lot more socks.

scenes.role: chương 1: con số mưa và so sánh đời thường
scenes.narration: Let me put the number on the table. The World Meteorological Organization records an average of about eleven thousand eight hundred and seventy-two millimetres of rain a year here. That's about four hundred and sixty-seven inches. Picture a glass that starts empty on New Year's Day and is left outside. By the end of the year, the water in it would stand taller than a three-storey house, roughly thirty-nine feet. In nineteen eighty-five, according to NASA, more than twenty-five metres fell in a single year. That's over a thousand inches. I tried this with a real glass on my first evening. Within an hour I needed a bucket. Within the next hour, I was mostly thinking about buying a boat.

scenes.role: chương 2: Wob đoán (gần biển) → cơ chế thật: gió mùa từ vịnh Bengal, đồng bằng, đồi chặn
scenes.narration: So why here? My guess was simple. It must be right next to the sea. It is not. The coast is a long way south. The real reason is the shape of the land. In the monsoon season, warm wet air comes off the Bay of Bengal and rolls north across the flat plains of Bangladesh. Nothing stops it. Then it hits these hills, which rise steeply to around fourteen hundred metres. The air is shoved upward, it cools, and the water in it falls out as rain. A scientist from the India Meteorological Department told AFP that moisture gathering over the Bay of Bengal is what gives Mawsynram its heavy, long monsoon. Think of the lid on a boiling pot. The steam hits the cool lid and drips. Mawsynram is the lid.

scenes.role: chương 3: Wob dùng ô → hỏng; knup: khiên tre mai rùa, rảnh tay làm ruộng dốc
scenes.narration: My first morning, I went out with an umbrella. A good one. The rain did not come down, it came sideways. My umbrella turned inside out, then outside in, then decided to leave. A woman walked past wearing what looked like a giant woven turtle shell on her head and back. Dry. Both hands free, carrying firewood. That shell is called a knup. Here's the clever part. It is woven from bamboo with layers of dried palm leaf, or these days sometimes plastic sheet, and it covers you from the head down to the knees. Because you do not hold it, you can work on steep terraced slopes with both hands. India's Ministry of Culture calls it a cultural symbol of Meghalaya. An umbrella is a hat you have to carry. A knup is a roof that walks with you.

scenes.role: phụ nữ đan knup trong mùa mưa; tre và cỏ chổi; Wob học đan; Wob đổi ý lần 1
scenes.narration: According to AFP, women here weave knups through the rainy season, from bamboo slivers, plastic sheets and broom grass, and each one takes at least an hour. Bamboo and broom grass are the main crops on these rocky hills. The broom grass is soaked, flattened and dried on rooftops, then made into brooms and baskets that traders carry across the state. I was given a knup to try for the afternoon. I walked to the edge of a terraced field and stood there in a downpour, perfectly dry, hands in my pockets, feeling like a very smug tortoise. For once on this trip, I thought, maybe. Maybe this works.

scenes.role: chương 4: từ một chiếc rễ tới cây cầu tới 72 làng; cầu rễ sống; UNESCO
scenes.narration: Then I went south, to the villages in the valleys below, to see the thing everyone had told me about. It starts with a single root. A thin root, hanging from a rubber fig tree beside a stream. Villagers guide roots like that across the water, tied along bamboo, until they reach the far bank and take hold. Zoom out: many roots, thickened and woven together into a bridge you can walk on. According to the United Nations Development Programme, growing one can take twenty to twenty-five years. Zoom out again. These living root bridges are found in seventy-two villages across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. Those villages were put on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in twenty twenty-two. In January twenty twenty-six, India formally submitted them for World Heritage status. Here's why they make sense. Wood rots fast in this much rain. A bridge that is alive keeps growing stronger. I crossed one very slowly, apologising to every root.

scenes.narration: Back in Mawsynram, I spent a whole day indoors, which is what the monsoon mostly asks of you. Morning: the noise. AFP reported that villagers thatch their roofs with grass to muffle the rain, though a heavy downpour can knock the grass loose. The village headman told AFP that during the monsoon, people have to talk a little louder to be heard. I said good morning. Nobody heard me. I said it again, louder. A cloud heard me. Mid-morning: the cloud came in. Clouds here sometimes drift right into homes and leave a wet film on the furniture. I watched one settle on my bed like a cat that had decided this was its spot now.

scenes.narration: Afternoon: the power went out. AFP reported that most homes now have electricity, but outages are common, and during the monsoon it gets very dark inside. Landslides regularly block the only paved road linking the hamlets. That is why every winter, people here repair their roofs and stack firewood for cooking and light. They store up food, because in the wettest months few people go out to shop. Evening: I ate by candlelight, listening to the rain play the roof like a drum kit with no off switch. My socks were drying by the fire. They were not drying. They were simply warm and wet now, which is worse. And here is my favourite detail. When the rains finally end, there is no festival. People just bring their clothes outside to dry. I respected that enormously. I also changed my mind. A monsoon here is not weather. It is a season you have to plan your whole year around, and I am not a planner.

scenes.chapter: Too Much Rain, Not Enough Water
scenes.role: chương 6: quay lại mùa khô; nghịch lý thiếu nước; vì sao
scenes.narration: I went back in the dry season, expecting to finally dry my socks. They dried. But I learned something that surprised me more than the rain. In these hills, the rain falls mostly in the monsoon months, and on steep, rocky slopes it runs off fast, down into the rivers and the plains. So in the dry months, water can run short. In nearby Cherrapunji, the India Water Portal reports, people buy water from tanker trucks, and streams that once ran all year now fall silent by winter. A recent study warns the risk of drought is growing, as rain comes in fewer, more intense bursts. Picture pouring a whole bucket onto a steep tin roof. It gets very wet, very fast, and keeps almost nothing. I stood by a dry stream bed in one of the rainiest corners of the planet, holding a bottle of water I had bought. It felt like a joke the landscape was telling on purpose.

scenes.role: vì sao người ta vẫn ở: quê, nghề, cộng đồng; lời trưởng làng (AFP)
scenes.narration: So why stay? I kept coming back to what the people here have built. A roof you can wear. A bridge that grows. Houses with steep roofs and deep eaves that throw water clear of the walls. A calendar where winter is for getting ready. This is the Khasi people's home, and they have shaped a whole way of life around the sky above it. The village headman told AFP he will never leave: he was born here, and he will die here. Nobody I met seemed to think the rain was a reason to go. It was simply the weather of home, the way snow is for some people, or traffic is for others. On my last evening I asked the rain, out loud, whether it ever got tired. It did not answer. It was busy. I took that as a no, and went inside to admire a roof that has heard that question many times.

scenes.chapter: Would I Move Into the Rain?
scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết NOPE, callback chiếc tất, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is how it all fits. Wet air from the Bay of Bengal crosses a flat plain and slams into these hills, and the sky empties itself here for months. The Khasi families who call it home answered with knups, grass roofs, root bridges and a year built around the monsoon. Would I move there? I admire it enormously. I would visit in the dry season and stare at the bridges for hours. But a cloud slept in my bed, and my socks are still damp. My verdict is NOPE, and the weakness is entirely mine. It suits patient people who like green hills, quiet evenings and talking a little louder. It does not suit anyone who owns only one pair of socks. I pinned the sock to my wall, next to the window. It is still dripping. How long would you last in a monsoon before you missed the sun?

verdict.label: NOPE
verdict.reason: Months of rain heavy enough to drown out conversation, clouds indoors and landslides on the only road are more than Wob can handle, even though the Khasi way of life has answered all of it.

claims.quote: It is woven from bamboo with layers of dried palm leaf, or these days sometimes plastic sheet, and it covers you from the head down to the knees. Because you do not hold it, you can work on steep terraced slopes with both hands. India's Ministry of Culture calls it a cultural symbol of Meghalaya.
claims.statement: The knup, a Khasi rain shield woven from bamboo with layers of palm leaf (sometimes plastic), protects the wearer from head to knees and leaves both hands free for work on steep terraced slopes; India's Ministry of Culture describes it as a cultural symbol of Meghalaya.

claims.quote: According to AFP, women here weave knups through the rainy season, from bamboo slivers, plastic sheets and broom grass, and each one takes at least an hour.
claims.statement: According to AFP, women in Mawsynram weave knups during the rainy season from bamboo slivers, plastic sheets and broom grass, each taking at least an hour.

claims.quote: Bamboo and broom grass are the main crops on these rocky hills. The broom grass is soaked, flattened and dried on rooftops, then made into brooms and baskets that traders carry across the state.
claims.statement: Bamboo and broom grass are the main plants grown around Mawsynram; broom grass is soaked, flattened and dried on rooftops, and baskets and brooms are sold by traders across Meghalaya.

claims.quote: Villagers guide roots like that across the water, tied along bamboo, until they reach the far bank and take hold.
claims.statement: Living root bridges are made by guiding the aerial roots of rubber fig trees (Ficus elastica) across streams along bamboo until they take hold on the other bank.

claims.quote: According to the United Nations Development Programme, growing one can take twenty to twenty-five years.
claims.statement: According to UNDP, growing a living root bridge can take 20 to 25 years.

claims.quote: These living root bridges are found in seventy-two villages across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. Those villages were put on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in twenty twenty-two. In January twenty twenty-six, India formally submitted them for World Heritage status.
claims.statement: Living root bridges in 72 villages of Meghalaya's Khasi and Jaintia Hills were placed on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in 2022, and India submitted their nomination dossier in January 2026.

claims.quote: Wood rots fast in this much rain. A bridge that is alive keeps growing stronger.
claims.statement: Living root bridges continue to grow and strengthen over time, unlike timber, which decays quickly in Meghalaya's wet climate.

claims.quote: AFP reported that villagers thatch their roofs with grass to muffle the rain, though a heavy downpour can knock the grass loose. The village headman told AFP that during the monsoon, people have to talk a little louder to be heard.
claims.statement: AFP reported that Mawsynram villagers thatch roofs with grass to muffle the rain, and the village headman said people have to talk louder to be heard during the monsoon.

claims.quote: Clouds here sometimes drift right into homes and leave a wet film on the furniture.
claims.statement: In Mawsynram, clouds sometimes drift into homes and leave a wet film on furniture.

claims.quote: AFP reported that most homes now have electricity, but outages are common, and during the monsoon it gets very dark inside. Landslides regularly block the only paved road linking the hamlets.
claims.statement: Most homes in Mawsynram now have electricity but outages are common, and landslides regularly block the only paved road linking its hamlets.

claims.quote: every winter, people here repair their roofs and stack firewood for cooking and light. They store up food, because in the wettest months few people go out to shop
claims.statement: Each winter Mawsynram residents repair roofs, stockpile firewood for cooking and light, and store food, because few go out to shop in the wettest months.

claims.quote: When the rains finally end, there is no festival. People just bring their clothes outside to dry.
claims.statement: When the monsoon ends in Mawsynram there is no festival; villagers simply begin drying their clothes outside.

claims.quote: In these hills, the rain falls mostly in the monsoon months, and on steep, rocky slopes it runs off fast, down into the rivers and the plains. So in the dry months, water can run short.
claims.statement: In Meghalaya's wettest hills most rain falls in the monsoon months and runs off steep, rocky terrain quickly, so seasonal water shortages occur in the dry months.

claims.quote: In nearby Cherrapunji, the India Water Portal reports, people buy water from tanker trucks, and streams that once ran all year now fall silent by winter. A recent study warns the risk of drought is growing, as rain comes in fewer, more intense bursts.
claims.statement: India Water Portal reports that residents of Cherrapunji (Sohra) buy water from tankers and streams that once flowed year-round dry up by winter; a recent study finds growing drought risk as rainfall becomes more intense with fewer rainy days.

claims.quote: Houses with steep roofs and deep eaves that throw water clear of the walls.
claims.statement: Traditional Khasi houses have steeply pitched roofs with deep overhangs that throw rainwater clear of the walls.

claims.quote: The village headman told AFP he will never leave: he was born here, and he will die here.
claims.statement: Mawsynram's village headman told AFP he would never leave because he was born there and would die there.
